article.source_body: 4 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Former NASA astronaut and Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman joins Caltech and NASA JPL as Caltech associate vice president and JPL deputy director on Nov. 30. Photo Credit: NASA Artemis II Commander Reid Wiseman has been named Caltech associate vice president and deputy director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The emeritus astronaut and retired U.S. Navy captain begins his new role at NASA’s center of excellence for robotics and deep space exploration and at Caltech, which manages JPL for NASA, on Nov. 30, 2026. “Reid has spent his career at the edge of what is possible, and he has the technical judgment, operational experience, and leadership to help push that edge farther,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “As commander of Artemis II, he helped carry America back around the Moon, and now, as an emeritus astronaut, he will continue giving back to NASA from a new vantage point at JPL. Reid is joining a storied laboratory that has made an enormous amount of history, and there is a lot more ahead. I am excited to see what he and the JPL team accomplish in the years to come.” During the Artemis II test flight, Wiseman , Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen journeyed 695,081 miles on a lunar flyby that took them farther than any humans have ever traveled before. “It feels fitting for Reid, who with the Artemis II crew traveled farther from Earth than any human in history, to join Caltech and JPL — institutions that for nearly 90 years have sent spacecraft into the far reaches of our solar system and beyond,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director and Caltech vice president. “Reid shares our drive for discovery, knows what it takes to lead teams through high-stakes missions, and has a remarkable ability to inspire people everywhere. He adds incredible bench strength to our leadership team as we build on the lab’s legacy and shape its future together.” After joining NASA’s astronaut corps in 2009, Wiseman went on to serve as flight engineer aboard the International Space Station for the 165-day Expedition 41 mission in 2014 and was a commander of NASA’s 21st Extreme Environment Mission Operations expedition, during which he lived for eight days in a habitat on the ocean floor in 2016. As the agency’s chief astronaut from December 2020 to November 2022, Wiseman led NASA’s astronaut corps, overseeing crew flight readiness and crew safety for all NASA human spaceflight missions. During his years of service at the agency, he has conducted hundreds of scientific experiments. “I’ve explored the furthest reaches of what a human can explore at NASA — and there were truly no words in the English vocabulary to describe seeing the Sun disappear behind the Moon from deep space. But that experience was really the jumping off point to go do the impossible things that Caltech and JPL dream, dare together, and do for NASA and the nation,” Wiseman said. “What an awesome time in my career to join this team and to try and push humanity and push our understanding of the solar system and the universe.” Wiseman joins JPL, NASA’s only federally funded research and development center, as the lab approaches its 90th anniversary since being founded by Caltech. In his role as Caltech’s associate vice president and JPL deputy director, Wiseman will be responsible for the strategic leadership, stewardship and continuous improvement of laboratory operations, including close partnership with Caltech on institutional planning, management and compliance. Serving as Center Management Authority for JPL mission execution, Wiseman will ensure operational excellence across mission support functions in accordance with NASA requirements and applicable federal and state regulations. In addition, he will be JPL’s primary interface for national security programs. “Reid brings to Caltech and JPL a truly unprecedented view of what humanity can achieve when ingenuity and determination are matched with the courage to pursue the furthest frontiers,” said Caltech president Ray Jayawardhana. “His pioneering spirit coupled with unbounded curiosity make him a natural fit for Caltech and JPL, a force-multiplier for a community whose daring continues to push the limits of humanity’s reach. I look forward to working closely with Dave and Reid as we chart our next era of exploration in partnership with NASA, elevating America’s space ambitions to breathtaking new heights.” After receiving a bachelor’s degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Wiseman joined the Navy, going on to fly combat missions and serve as a test pilot. article.description: La vista de un rostro helado parecido a un cráneo en la isla antártica podría hacer que la sangre se te helara.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Isla Vega Congelada en Terror**

En un inquietante hallazgo, imágenes satelitales de la isla Vega, ubicada en el mar de Weddell, han revelado que parte de su superficie helada presenta la apariencia de un cráneo sonriente. Este fenómeno, observado por primera vez en marzo de 2025 y nuevamente en octubre de 2026, ha sido documentado por el Earth Observatory de la NASA. La transformación de la isla se debe a la exposición de hielo desnudo, resultado de temperaturas inusualmente altas durante el invierno de 2026.

El glaciólogo Mauri Pelto, de Nichols College, señala que la falta de acumulación de nieve y el efecto de la sublimación han contribuido a la disminución de la masa de hielo en la isla. Las imágenes muestran un contraste notable entre la capa de nieve en marzo y la ausencia de esta en octubre, lo que sugiere un acelerado proceso de derretimiento. Este fenómeno no solo afecta la morfología de la isla, sino que también plantea preocupaciones sobre el futuro de los glaciares en la región.

La isla Vega tiene una historia trágica, siendo parte de la expedición antártica sueca de 1901-1903, donde los exploradores enfrentaron condiciones extremas. Hoy, el cambio climático amenaza con alterar aún más este paisaje helado, lo que podría tener repercusiones significativas en el ecosistema antártico.

Some of the face has a gray appearance where seasonal snow is gone and bare ice is exposed. NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin March 22, 2025 October 10, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island. These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) A nunatak jutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, a lateral moraine forms a mouth, and Bahía del Diablo (Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible. Above-average temperatures in winter 2026 —particularly in June —were partly responsible for so much bare ice in October , said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.” The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.” October 10, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In a study published in 1982 , scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega. Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has been closely monitored since the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring an overall decline in its mass. Satellite images acquired in recent decades show ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock. Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, they lost their ship to the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal. NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . article.description: El súper tifón In-fa desarrolló un ojo inusualmente grande, y los remanentes del tifón Champi se transformaron en una tormenta extratropical que se dirigió a Alaska.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: La movida temporada de tormentas del Pacífico**

La temporada de tormentas en el Pacífico ha mostrado una actividad inusualmente alta desde abril de 2026, cuando el tifón Sinlaku alcanzó la categoría de supertifón y causó estragos en Micronesia, Guam y las Islas Marianas del Norte. Hasta finales de octubre, se han registrado 25 tormentas nombradas, destacando el Super Tifón In-fa, que se encontraba activo cerca de las Islas Marianas el 29 de octubre.

In-fa es el quinto tifón que afecta a las Islas Marianas este año y se caracteriza por su forma casi circular y un gran ojo, lo que lo clasifica como una tormenta anular, un fenómeno raro que representa solo el 4% de los ciclones tropicales en el noroeste del Pacífico. Estas tormentas tienden a mantener su intensidad durante más tiempo, incluso en condiciones desfavorables.

Por otro lado, los restos del tifón Champi se acercaron a Alaska, donde se reportaron vientos fuertes y lluvias intensas, aunque sin causar daños catastróficos. Este año, Alaska ha recibido cuatro ex-tifones, un fenómeno que se ha vuelto más común debido a un fuerte El Niño, que ha influido en la trayectoria de las tormentas, llevándolas hacia el norte en lugar de continuar su camino hacia Asia.

article.original_title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October. When the EPIC (Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera) on the DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory) satellite captured this image (above) on October 29, 2026, Super Typhoon In-fa churned near the Mariana Islands. At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea. In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured the image of In-fa below on October 30, when the storm was just west of the island chain. In-fa was unusually intense at the time of the image, with a nearly circular shape and large eye—a collection of characteristics that meteorologists use to identify a subset of tropical cyclones known as annular storms . These storms typically lack prominent outer spiral-shaped rainbands—a common feature of standard tropical cyclones—which is why meteorologists have a habit of calling annular storms “doughnuts” or “truck tires.” Annular storms are rare, accounting for just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, according to one analysis . Their eyes average about 45 kilometers (30 miles) in diameter, compared to about 25 kilometers for standard tropical cyclones, and the storms typically maintain their strength longer in unfavorable conditions. In-fa was still a tropical cyclone when EPIC captured the image at the top of the page, but Champi’s leftovers had gone through the process of extratropical transition and become a whole different type of storm as they entered the Bering Sea’s busy storm track. Tropical cyclones are warm-core storms fueled by the heat and moisture of warm ocean water, but extratropical cyclones typically have cold cores and draw energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses. Unlike tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones typically develop fronts and huge, spiraling cloud bands shaped like commas . “One of the calling cards of extratropical transitions is the expansion of a storm’s wind field,” said Gary Partyka, a meteorologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “It’s not that the winds necessarily grow stronger, but they cover a much larger area,” he said. In this case, there likely would still have been a midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, possibly with large, comma-shaped clouds on October 30, even without Champi’s remnants, he added. “But it looks like Champi became intertwined with and helped intensify that system,” he said. Champi’s transformation came after a long and destructive tour through the West Pacific, during which the typhoon achieved maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers (185 miles) per hour, prompting some observers to call it one of the strongest storms of the season. Despite narrowly skirting Taiwan and Guam, the powerhouse storm brought damaging winds and intense rains to both places, as well as to parts of China and Japan. When the remnants hit Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage on the scale of what happened after ex-typhoon Halong struck in October 2025 , but some areas did see high winds and heavy rain and snowfall, according to news reports . Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, noted University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist and climatologist Rick Thoman , following Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October. The autumns of 1997 and 2015—both very strong El Niño years—had three each, he added. Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have impacted the state since 1970 , according to Thoman. Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the chances that Alaska would be affected by storms that have gone through extratropical transitions. The strong El Niño underway in the Pacific is a “likely contributor” to the increased activity, he added. El Niño is a climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years, marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. In the Northwest Pacific, the phenomenon tends to cause storms to more readily curve northward rather than continuing westward to East Asia and Southeast Asia, some experts say , bringing more storms toward Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula. article.description: Los científicos han descubierto que el magma en el interior de la Tierra puede almacenar sorprendentes cantidades de oxígeno adicional, lo que podría revelar un contribuyente oculto a la atmósfera rica en oxígeno de nuestro planeta. Los hallazgos sugieren que antiguas erupciones volcánicas pueden haber ayudado a transformar la atmósfera de la Tierra hace miles de millones de años, con implicaciones para entender la vida en otros planetas.
article.explanation:
**Científicos descubren un reservorio de oxígeno oculto en las profundidades de la Tierra**

Investigadores han revelado que el magma en las profundidades de la Tierra puede almacenar mucho más oxígeno de lo que se pensaba anteriormente. Este hallazgo, liderado por el Dr. Yanhao Lin y el Dr. Ho-kwang Mao del Centro de Ciencia y Tecnología de Alta Presión (HPSTAR), desafía creencias arraigadas sobre la composición del magma y sugiere que el oxígeno liberado desde el interior del planeta pudo haber influido en la transformación de la atmósfera terrestre hace miles de millones de años.

A través de experimentos de alta presión y simulaciones computacionales, los científicos descubrieron que el magma puede absorber oxígeno adicional, más allá de lo que su composición química habitual permitiría. En condiciones extremas, como presiones de hasta 7 gigapascales y temperaturas entre 1200 y 1800 °C, se encontró que el oxígeno adicional podía representar más del 5% del peso de las muestras analizadas.

Este descubrimiento plantea interrogantes sobre el papel del magma en la historia de la Tierra, sugiriendo que podría haber transportado oxígeno desde el interior hacia la superficie, contribuyendo así a la oxidación de la atmósfera. Los investigadores estiman que, si el magma liberara solo el 0.27% de su peso en oxígeno, podría igualar la cantidad total de oxígeno presente en la atmósfera actual. Estos hallazgos podrían tener implicaciones significativas en la comprensión de la evolución atmosférica de la Tierra y otros planetas rocosos.

article.description: Un registro de altimetría satelital de 35 años permite a los científicos comparar el fenómeno de El Niño de este año con sus predecesores más fuertes.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: El Niño antes y ahora**

En octubre de 2026, los niveles del mar en el Pacífico ecuatorial central y oriental son más altos de lo normal, un fenómeno característico del evento de El Niño. Este patrón se asemeja al observado en octubre de 1997, durante uno de los eventos más intensos registrados en la historia de la altimetría satelital. Según datos de la NASA, la comparación entre ambos años muestra un aumento significativo en la temperatura del agua y la altura del nivel del mar.

El fenómeno de El Niño, que ocurre cada dos a siete años, trae consigo un calentamiento de las aguas del Pacífico, alterando patrones climáticos globales. Los eventos de 1997-98 y 2015-16 causaron estragos en diversas regiones, desde incendios en Indonesia hasta inundaciones en California. Actualmente, se prevé que el evento de 2026 sea comparable en magnitud a estos anteriores, con un 83% de probabilidad de que se mantenga fuerte hasta principios de 2027.

Josh Willis, científico del Laboratorio de Propulsión a Chorro de la NASA, advierte que, aunque el fenómeno actual presenta similitudes con el de 1997, cada evento tiene características únicas que pueden influir en sus impactos climáticos. La incertidumbre persiste, y se espera que los efectos de El Niño se sientan en diversas partes del mundo, incluyendo Chile, donde podrían intensificarse las lluvias y afectar la agricultura.

Maps by NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin using altimetry data provided by NASA/JPL-Caltech. El Niño is part of a natural climate pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years, bringing warmer-than-normal water to parts of the equatorial Pacific. The most recent very strong El Niño events, in 1997-98 and 2015-16, upended weather patterns. Impacts spanned the planet, from fires in Indonesia and the Amazon, to crop failures due to drought in southern Africa , to heavy rain and coastal flooding in Southern California. The current El Niño rivals these past heavyweights. Every El Niño grows from a feedback loop between the atmosphere and the ocean. Trade winds normally keep warm water piled up in the western Pacific, where it stands higher than in the east. When those winds weaken, that warm water begins to pulse eastward, which further weakens and sometimes reverses the winds, allowing even more warm water to move east. The cycle intensifies as waters continue to warm and pile up in the central and eastern Pacific. But each El Niño has its own character, shaped by where in the Pacific the warmth builds and how the atmosphere responds. “The search for the ‘typical’ El Niño is very elusive,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). “They’re all different in terms of where they land and how their impacts play out.” Altimetry satellites can track those differences by measuring the height of the sea surface. Because water expands as it warms, higher-than-normal sea levels in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific signal the buildup of heat associated with El Niño. The maps above depict sea surface height anomalies across the Pacific Ocean on October 13, 1997 (left), and on October 12, 2026 (right). Data are from the TOPEX/Poseidon satellite and the Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich satellite, respectively, and were processed by scientists at JPL. Shades of red indicate where sea levels were higher than average. Normal sea level conditions appear white, and lower areas are blue. Signals related to seasonal cycles and long-term trends have been removed to highlight sea level anomalies associated with El Niño and other short-term natural phenomena. “What’s unique about altimetry is that we have a 35-year record from nearly identical satellites flying almost the same ground track, with each mission overlapping the next,” Willis said. “That lets us look back in time and compare this El Niño to what happened in 1997. And right now, this one is on track to be even bigger.” Compared with the 1997-98 event, El Niño in 2026 came on much more suddenly. But as of October, the two events appear similar in character—the tilt of sea level (low in the west and high in the east) and high, warm water extending all the way to South America—so Willis thinks the impacts could be similar as well. In 1997-98, that meant, for instance, lots of rain in California and across the southern tier of the U.S. The 2015-16 El Niño was also very strong, as elevated sea levels in October 2015 (middle) show. But its pattern differed from those in October 1997 (top) and October 2026 (bottom): less of the elevated water reached the coast of South America, which contributed to different weather patterns that year. The 2015-16 El Niño was another heavy hitter but differed in its character. Sea surface height anomalies on October 12, 2015, based on altimetry data from the Jason-2 satellite, are shown above in context with maps from around the same time in 1997 and 2026. In 2015, the exceptionally warm, high water along the equator didn’t push up against South America to the extent it did in the other years. Rainfall impacts that winter concentrated more over Central America and the southeastern U.S., with significant flooding in Mexico. NOAA’s El Niño outlook on October 8, 2026, called for an 83 percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño through the first three months of 2027. But exactly how the impacts will play out in winter 2026-27 and beyond remains to be seen. Willis noted that El Niño’s influence propagates through a chaotic atmosphere, and the signal can get muddled as it extends beyond the tropics. “There’s always a bit of a dice roll here,” Willis said. “Just because this El Niño looks like 1997 doesn’t mean it will be exactly the same—it’s just our best guess at the moment.” NASA Earth Observatory maps by Lauren Dauphin, using NASA-SSH altimetry data provided by Josh Willis, Severine Fournier, and Kevin Marlis, NASA/JPL-Caltech. article.description: Profundamente bajo la caldera Kikai de Japón, un masivo reservorio de magma se está reabasteciendo 7,300 años después de una de las erupciones volcánicas más poderosas en la reciente historia geológica de la Tierra. Los científicos utilizaron encuestas sísmicas submarinas para revelar un vasto almacén de magma que parece haberse acumulado desde la antigua catástrofe. El descubrimiento podría ayudar a explicar cómo los supervolcanes como Yellowstone y Toba reconstruyen sus suministros de magma.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Uno de los supervolcanes más poderosos de la Tierra se está rellenando con magma fresco**

Investigadores de la Universidad de Kobe han descubierto que el supervolcán Kikai, ubicado en Japón, está acumulando magma fresco en su enorme reservorio subterráneo, miles de años después de una de las erupciones más devastadoras de la historia geológica reciente. Esta erupción ocurrió hace aproximadamente 7,300 años y fue la más grande del Holoceno.

El estudio, publicado en Communications Earth & Environment, revela que el magma actual no es simplemente material residual de la erupción anterior. Se ha identificado un nuevo domo de lava en desarrollo en el centro de la caldera, lo que sugiere que el magma proviene de inyecciones recientes de roca fundida desde las profundidades de la corteza terrestre. Los investigadores utilizaron técnicas sísmicas avanzadas para mapear el reservorio, encontrando una región significativa con alta proporción de magma justo debajo del sitio de la erupción histórica.

Este hallazgo no indica que una nueva erupción sea inminente, sino que proporciona una visión crucial sobre cómo los supervolcanes pueden recargar sus reservas de magma a lo largo de miles de años. Comprender este proceso es vital para anticipar el comportamiento de otros supervolcanes, como Yellowstone y Toba.

article.explanation:
Frente a la costa de la Isla de Vancouver, se ha observado que una placa oceánica está en proceso de desintegración. Este fenómeno ha permitido a los científicos obtener una visión más clara de una zona de subducción que se encuentra en un estado de deterioro. Las zonas de subducción son áreas donde una placa tectónica se desliza por debajo de otra, y su estudio es crucial para entender los procesos geológicos que ocurren en el fondo marino.

La desintegración de esta placa oceánica ofrece una oportunidad única para investigar cómo estas zonas pueden cambiar con el tiempo y qué implica su "muerte" en términos geológicos. Este tipo de investigación es fundamental para ampliar nuestro conocimiento sobre la dinámica de la Tierra y los procesos que afectan la formación y destrucción de las placas tectónicas.

article.explanation:
Blade Resources ha decidido aumentar en un 39% el alcance de su estudio geofísico en Arizona, con el objetivo de identificar nuevos depósitos de cobre y oro en la región. Esta ampliación del estudio refleja el interés de la empresa en explorar más a fondo el potencial mineral de la zona, que es conocida por su riqueza en recursos naturales.

El estudio geofísico es una herramienta clave en la minería, ya que permite a las empresas obtener información sobre la composición del subsuelo sin necesidad de realizar excavaciones extensivas. Al ampliar este estudio, Blade Resources busca mejorar su comprensión de la geología local y localizar áreas que podrían ser económicamente viables para la extracción de metales preciosos.

Este movimiento se enmarca dentro de una tendencia más amplia en la industria minera, donde las empresas están invirtiendo en tecnología y estudios geofísicos para optimizar sus operaciones y maximizar la eficiencia en la búsqueda de recursos.

article.explanation: Una masiva erupción volcánica que golpeó Japón hace unos 7,300 años tuvo un impacto devastador en las comunidades prehistóricas, pero sus consecuencias fueron mucho más complicadas de lo que los científicos creían anteriormente. Mientras que algunas poblaciones disminuyeron o desaparecieron de las áreas afectadas, otras continuaron creciendo a pesar de la destrucción. Un equipo de investigación internacional liderado por la Universidad de Lund investigó cómo la erupción Kikai-Akahoya cambió los patrones de población en Japón. Sus hallazgos desafían la idea de que el desastre o bien aniquiló completamente a las comunidades cercanas o las dejó en gran medida sin afectar. En cambio, los investigadores descubrieron una sorprendente mezcla de disminución de la población, migración, adaptación y crecimiento. Cuando el volcán Kikai-Akahoya erupcionó bajo el mar aproximadamente hace 7,300 años, Japón era hogar de comunidades Jomon que dependían de la caza y la recolección para sobrevivir. "Esta erupción debió ser devastadora, explotando desde el lecho marino con poca advertencia. Golpeó las islas japonesas con poderosos terremotos y enormes tsunamis, y luego cubrió el paisaje con metros de ceniza volcánica", explica el autor principal Peter Jordan, profesor de arqueología en la Universidad de Lund.

article.description: La primera tormenta nombrada de la temporada de ciclones del océano Índico norte tocó tierra a lo largo de la costa de Andhra Pradesh.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Ciclón Arnab Devasta la Costa Este de India**

El ciclón Arnab, la primera tormenta nombrada de la temporada de ciclones del Océano Índico Norte 2026, se formó en la Bahía de Bengala el 25 de octubre. Con vientos sostenidos de hasta 140 kilómetros por hora, el fenómeno meteorológico tocó tierra en la costa de Andhra Pradesh y Yanam el 28 de octubre, donde se registraron vientos de 130 kilómetros por hora, clasificándose como un "ciclón muy severo" según el Departamento Meteorológico de India (IMD).

La tormenta impactó entre Bapatla y Visakhapatnam, una región densamente poblada que alberga grandes ciudades y comunidades pesqueras. Arnab causó daños extensos, derribando árboles, inundando cultivos y hogares, y afectando las operaciones pesqueras y las redes de transporte y energía. Las autoridades indias evacuaron a más de 84,000 personas de áreas costeras vulnerables antes de la llegada del ciclón.

Este evento se produce en el contexto de un fenómeno de El Niño, que altera las condiciones oceánicas y puede influir en la actividad ciclónica. A pesar de que se espera una reducción en la frecuencia e intensidad de los ciclones durante años de El Niño, Arnab ha demostrado ser una excepción significativa, dejando a su paso un saldo de al menos tres víctimas fatales y una devastación considerable en la región.
article.original_title: Arnab Strikes India
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Arnab Strikes India Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search The first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season—Arnab (pronounced Or-nab)—emerged in the Bay of Bengal on October 25, a rather late start for a basin that typically produces named cyclones in April or May. When the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-20 captured this nighttime image at 20:12 Universal Time on October 26 (1:42 a.m. India Standard Time on October 27), the storm had sustained winds of about 140 kilometers (85 miles) per hour, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). When Arnab made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early on October 28, sustained winds were 130 kilometers per hour. IMD categorizes a storm that strength as a “very severe cyclonic storm ,” which is similar to a Category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson hurricane wind scale . It made landfall between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, a heavily settled area home to large cities, farmland, and fishing communities. Arnab caused extensive damage, uprooting trees, inundating crops and homes, limiting fishing operations, and disrupting transportation and power networks, according to news reports . Prior to landfall, Indian authorities had evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas. The storm comes in the midst of an El Niño , a climate pattern marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific that emerges roughly every two to seven years. The changed ocean conditions can influence the atmosphere in ways that alter global weather patterns and change the distribution of rainfall, winds, tropical cyclones, fires, floods, and other phenomena. In the Bay of Bengal, for instance, some research indicates that altered environmental conditions during an El Niño are associated with a reduction in tropical cyclone activity. The ocean basin sees both less frequent and less intense tropical cyclones during El Niño years, researchers have found. article.source_body: Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft is pictured on Oct. 9, 2026, in the grip of the Canadarm2 robotic arm moments before its release into Earth orbit after a nearly six‑month stay attached to the International Space Station’s Unity module. The orbital outpost was soaring 263 miles above the Indian Ocean, off the coast of Madagascar, at the time of this photograph. Credit: NASA Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA. Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U.S. media. The application deadline for U.S. citizens is 11:59 p.m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at: https://media.ksc.nasa.gov Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail.nasa.gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468. In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions. Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U.S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space. For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy , NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars. article.explanation:
**TITULAR: ¿Qué pasa?: Consejos de la NASA para observar el cielo en noviembre de 2026**

**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

Noviembre de 2026 promete ser un mes emocionante para los amantes de la astronomía en Chile, con una serie de eventos celestiales destacados. Entre ellos, se encuentran las lluvias de meteoros Taurids y Leonids, así como la aparición de una superluna.

El pico de las Taurids del Sur se espera alrededor del 5 de noviembre, seguido por las Taurids del Norte el 12 de noviembre, donde se podrán observar hasta cinco meteoros por hora en condiciones ideales. Para los observadores, se recomienda encontrar un lugar oscuro y permitir que los ojos se adapten a la oscuridad.

Un evento notable ocurrirá entre el 15 y 16 de noviembre, cuando Marte y Júpiter se alineen a solo 1.2 grados de distancia antes del amanecer, ofreciendo una vista espectacular. 

Además, el 17 de noviembre, la sonda Voyager 1 alcanzará un hito histórico al estar a un día luz de la Tierra, lo que significa que la señal tarda 24 horas en llegar a ella. Este evento será celebrado con la actividad "Shine Bright for Voyager".

Finalmente, el 24 de noviembre, los chilenos podrán disfrutar de una superluna, la primera de tres consecutivas, que promete iluminar el cielo nocturno.

article.source_body: Skywatching Skywatching Home What’s Up Meteor Showers Eclipses Daily Moon Guide More Tips & Guides Skywatching FAQ Night Sky Network Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon. Skywatching Highlights Around Nov. 5: Southern Taurids peak; occasional bright fireballs Around Nov. 12: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 15-16: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise Nov. 17: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation Nov. 17-18: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 24: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons A full Moon rises over Vasquez Rocks Natural Area and Nature Center north of Los Angeles, California, on June 24, 2021. Credit: NASA/Preston Dyches Transcript A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon! That’s What’s Up for November. November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky! The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th. Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate. Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile. A sky chart showing where to look for the Leonids in November 2026. NASA/JPL-Caltech Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer. To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can. Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together. A sky chart showing Mars and Jupiter close in the night sky. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby. Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side. Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways. Artist’s rendering of a NASA Voyager spacecraft traveling through interstellar space. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth. That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it! If you want to imagine where Voyager 1 is currently traveling, look in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. A night sky chart highlights the location of Voyager 1 within the constellation Ophiuchus on November 17 around 5 p.m., looking toward the western horizon. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech And on November 17th, join us in celebrating this milestone by participating in our Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation. Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager . On November 24th, the evening sky will be lit by a supermoon. Because the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, its distance from Earth changes. When it’s closer, the full Moon appears larger and brighter than average – though the difference can be subtle. This kicks off a series of three consecutive supermoons in November, December, and January. Look east around sunset to watch it rise. It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion —a common effect with any full Moon. Here are the phases of the Moon for November: Moon phases for November 2026, showing the dates for Third Quarter, New Moon, First Quarter, Full “Supermoon,” and a concluding Third Quarter in Pacific Time. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech You can stay up to date on all of NASA’s missions exploring the solar system and beyond at NASA Science . I’m Raquel Villanueva from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and that’s What’s Up this month. **TITULAR: Ciclón extratropical azota Islandia a su paso**

Un ciclón extratropical, originado a partir de los restos del huracán Isaias, ha impactado Islandia con fuerza, dejando a su paso vientos huracanados y condiciones climáticas severas. El fenómeno meteorológico se intensificó rápidamente, con una caída de presión de más de 50 hectopascales en solo 24 horas, lo que podría haber establecido un nuevo récord de presión barométrica para octubre en el país, superando una marca que se mantenía desde 1963.

El 14 de octubre de 2026, el ciclón tocó la costa islandesa, registrando ráfagas de hasta 205 kilómetros por hora cerca del volcán Eyjafjallajökull. En una pequeña isla cercana, se reportaron vientos sostenidos de 150 kilómetros por hora. Las condiciones adversas no solo afectaron el sur de Islandia, sino que también se extendieron hacia el norte, donde los residentes enfrentaron aguanieve y nieve.

Además, el impacto del ciclón se sintió en el noroeste de Escocia, donde se registraron ráfagas de hasta 90 kilómetros por hora, lo que provocó la cancelación de varias rutas de ferry. Este evento meteorológico resalta la creciente intensidad de los fenómenos climáticos en la región, generando preocupación entre los meteorólogos y las autoridades locales.

article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Extratropical Cyclone Whips… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Hurricane Isaias—the only Atlantic hurricane to date in 2026—made landfall in Florida as a Category 2 storm on October 9. After delivering a rainy, windy blow to the U.S. Gulf Coast and drenching much of the Eastern Seaboard, the weather system had more in store. Riding the jet stream east over the North Atlantic, Isaias’s remnants developed into a powerful storm known as an extratropical cyclone . These low-pressure systems often feature asymmetrical, comma-shaped cloud patterns and can strike with hurricane-force winds, rain, and blizzard-like conditions. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-21 satellite captured this image of the extratropical cyclone brushing past Iceland on the afternoon of October 14. During its journey, the system’s air pressure plummeted by more than 50 hectopascals over a 24-hour period, according to reports —approximately double the criteria for explosive cyclogenesis, or bombogenesis . Some meteorologists believe the storm may have set a new October low for barometric pressure in Iceland, after correcting for altitude, likely breaking a record that has stood since 1963. The cyclone lashed Iceland with high winds as it grazed the coast. A gust of 205 kilometers (128 miles) per hour was recorded near Eyjafjallajökull volcano in the country’s south, while a small island just offshore saw sustained winds of 150 kilometers (93 miles) per hour. Damaging winds extended into northern parts of the country, where residents also braced for sleet and snow. Farther across the Atlantic, northwestern Scotland received gusts up to 90 kilometers (55 miles) per hour on October 14, according to news reports , resulting in cancellations on several ferry routes. Investigadores de la NASA están descubriendo docenas de incendios previamente no detectados, lo que sugiere que la destrucción podría ser incluso más extensa de lo que muestran los registros satelitales.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: La NASA descubre incendios ocultos ardiendo bajo la selva amazónica**

La selva amazónica enfrenta una crisis creciente debido a una ola de incendios forestales, exacerbada por la sequía severa vinculada al fenómeno de El Niño. Desde septiembre de 2026, se ha observado un aumento significativo en la actividad de incendios y emisiones de humo en la región central y oriental de la Amazonía, especialmente alrededor de Manaus y Santarém, dos importantes centros comerciales en Brasil.

El 12 de octubre de 2026, imágenes del satélite Aqua de la NASA mostraron grandes columnas de humo elevándose a ambos lados del río Amazonas, afectando gravemente la calidad del aire en Manaus, donde las concentraciones de material particulado PM2.5 superaron los 135 microgramos por metro cúbico. Esto colocó a la ciudad en la segunda categoría más alta de un índice de calidad del aire regional, provocando el cierre de escuelas y la cancelación de eventos públicos.

Douglas Morton, científico del sistema terrestre en el Centro de Vuelo Espacial Goddard de la NASA, advirtió que estos incendios son parte de un patrón más amplio, donde la sequía en Indonesia inicia un efecto dominó que afecta a la Amazonía. Con condiciones de sequía extrema, se estima que entre 50 y 70 incendios no controlados están activos en la zona de Santarém, lo que podría indicar un número aún mayor de incendios no detectados por los sistemas de monitoreo convencionales.

article.explanation:
**TITULAR: Estado Actual del ISAM de la NASA: El Estándar de la Industria para el Servicio, Ensamblaje y Fabricación en el Espacio**

El In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) de la NASA ha alcanzado un hito significativo en su desarrollo, según el último informe publicado en octubre de 2026. Este documento, que abarca 368 páginas, detalla las capacidades actuales de ISAM en 11 áreas funcionales, incluyendo manipulación robótica y reabastecimiento, y se ha convertido en un recurso esencial para la industria espacial.

Desde su lanzamiento en 2021, el ISAM State of Play ha evolucionado, reflejando un crecimiento exponencial en el campo. Dale Arney, líder del equipo de tecnología ISAM en el Centro de Investigación Langley de la NASA, destacó que el documento no solo sirve como una enciclopedia, sino también como una hoja de ruta para las tecnologías que permitirán el servicio y ensamblaje de naves espaciales en órbita.

El informe se basa en criterios estrictos de entrada, asegurando que solo se incluyan tecnologías que existan físicamente, ya sea como prototipos en tierra o demostraciones en vuelo. Esto garantiza que el ISAM State of Play sea un recurso confiable para empresas que buscan entender y participar en este ecosistema en expansión.

Con la mirada puesta en misiones futuras más ambiciosas, el ISAM State of Play se posiciona como un documento clave que proporciona un vocabulario compartido y una base de capacidades necesarias para el desarrollo de infraestructuras lunares y manufactura en órbita.

article.source_body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) When companies began approaching NASA’s Langley Research Center, asking to be included in the In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) State of Play for access to competitive intelligence, the team knew they had crossed an inflection point. “We’ve had some unnamed companies ask if we have any proprietary information,” says Dale Arney, senior team lead for the ISAM Technology Portfolio at NASA Langley. The answer is “no,” but that impartiality is precisely what makes the State of Play invaluable to an industry trying to understand a rapidly expanding field. The cover of the ISAM State of Play, featuring Astronaut F. Story Musgrave, anchored on the Space Shuttle Endeavor’s robotic arm, preparing to be elevated to the top of the Hubble Space Telescope during Hubble’s first servicing mission in 1993. Credit: NASA Published since 2021, the 2026 edition has grown to 368 pages documenting current ISAM capabilities across 11 functional areas, from robotic manipulation to refueling and structural assembly. The document serves as both encyclopedia and roadmap for the technologies that will enable spacecraft to be serviced, assembled, and manufactured in orbit rather than launched as integrated systems. “The field itself has expanded more than linearly since we started,” Arney explains. What began as a tool to ensure NASA centers shared a common reference point has become the industry’s go-to resource for understanding what’s possible versus what’s still conceptual. The State of Play team maintains strict entry criteria: hardware must physically exist, either as ground prototypes or in-flight demonstrations. “We get people who will send their PowerPoint presentation of their technology idea,” Arney notes. “There’s no real indication they’ve done any work on the technology itself yet.” Those concepts don’t make the cut until the following year’s review. This rigor matters, because ISAM capabilities will enable missions impossible with traditional single-launch approaches. Future missions will require telescopes larger than any launch vehicle fairing, persistent national security assets that are mobile and resilient, and commercial systems that can upgrade to the latest technology on orbit without full replacement. The document is intentionally collaborative. “We like to refer to it as kind of a crowdsource document,” says team member John Mulvaney. Each year brings more interviews with industry partners to ensure accuracy and completeness. Contributions come from NASA centers including Ames, Glenn, Marshall, Kennedy, and Johnson, along with international developers meeting the hardware criteria. The result is more than a technical reference. The 2026 edition includes developer profiles and facilities documentation, providing mission designers with not just what’s possible but who’s doing it and where the work happens. For companies entering the ISAM ecosystem or expanding their capabilities, it offers both competitive context and collaboration opportunities. As the space industry moves toward more ambitious missions, from lunar infrastructure to on-orbit manufacturing, the ISAM State of Play provides the shared vocabulary and capability baseline that emerging ecosystems require. It’s not speculation about the future; it’s documentation of what exists now and where the hardware is heading next. article.explanation: El Ártico podría perder aproximadamente un millón de kilómetros cuadrados más de hielo marino invernal de lo que los científicos habían predicho anteriormente, según una nueva investigación que se basa en evidencia de un Ártico más cálido hace 6,000 años. Al utilizar registros climáticos antiguos para refinar los modelos computacionales modernos, los investigadores han producido estimaciones más confiables sobre cuánto hielo podría desaparecer en las próximas décadas. Los hallazgos, publicados en Nature Geoscience, también podrían tener importantes consecuencias para el clima invernal en el Reino Unido y otras partes de Europa. Gran parte de la atención en torno a la pérdida de hielo en el Ártico se ha centrado en el dramático retroceso del hielo marino en verano. Sin embargo, el hielo invernal ha recibido considerablemente menos escrutinio, a pesar de que los modelos climáticos muestran sus mayores desacuerdos al predecir cuánto hielo cubrirá el Ártico durante los meses más fríos. El hielo marino invernal influye en el clima mucho más allá del Ártico al controlar cuánto calor y humedad escapan del océano a la atmósfera. La disminución de la cobertura de hielo se ha asociado con inviernos más fríos y un aumento de las nevadas en el Reino Unido, el norte de Europa y América del Norte.

article.description: Un monumento nacional desde la década de 1920, Chiricahua es el parque nacional más nuevo de América.
article.explanation:
**TITULAR: La Tierra de las Rocas de Pie**

**CATEGORÍA: volcanes**

Un nuevo estudio geológico ha revelado la fascinante historia del Parque Nacional Chiricahua, ubicado en el sureste de Arizona, Estados Unidos. Hace aproximadamente 27 millones de años, un volcán en esta región provocó una serie de erupciones explosivas que dispersaron más de 1,000 veces la cantidad de material volcánico que el Monte St. Helens en 1980. Este evento dejó una huella geológica significativa, creando la caldera de Turkey Creek, que mide aproximadamente 19 kilómetros de ancho y 1,500 metros de profundidad.

Las erupciones generaron flujos piroclásticos que se solidificaron en depósitos de toba riolítica, formando impresionantes formaciones rocosas que hoy se conocen como "las rocas de pie". La erosión y el desgaste han esculpido este paisaje en un laberinto de pináculos y cañones, convirtiéndolo en un destino turístico popular.

Designado como monumento nacional en 1924 y posteriormente como Parque Nacional en octubre de 2026, Chiricahua alberga una rica biodiversidad, con más de 1,000 especies de plantas que prosperan en sus diversos ecosistemas. Este parque no solo preserva su geología única, sino que también se ha convertido en un refugio para la flora y fauna de la región.
article.original_title: The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks
article.source_body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Some 27 million years ago, a volcano in what’s now southeastern Arizona unleashed a spectacular series of eruptions, strewing more than 1,000 times as much volcanic material across the landscape as Mount St. Helens did in 1980. The explosive eruptions blanketed the region, part of the Chiricahua Apache Nation’s traditional lands, with ash and pumice . Layered into this were massive pyroclastic flows that hardened into deposits of welded rhyolitic tuff that in some areas were nearly 1,600 feet (500 meters) thick, about three times the height of the Washington Monument. As the magma chamber emptied, the ground above it collapsed, leaving a gaping depression—the Turkey Creek caldera —that was roughly 12 miles (19 kilometers) wide and 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) deep. An array of geologic processes, including erosion and weathering , gradually sculpted the welded layer of tuff into the collection of dramatic spires, hoodoos , and canyons that visitors to the caldera area encounter today. The Apache called the area “ The Land of the Standing-Up Rocks ” for good reason. Hiking through Rhyolite Canyon or driving through Bonita Canyon means encountering a dizzying maze of rock pinnacles, some hundreds of feet tall. Others, like Big Balanced Rock , have surprisingly large boulders precariously perched on top. Meanwhile, those at Heart of Rocks and Massai Point are gathered into groups of hundreds. The area was designated a national monument in 1924 to preserve its remarkable geology. In October 2026, it was redesignated as Chiricahua National Park (pronounced cheery-cow-ah ). The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this cloud-free image of the new national park on July 2, 2026. Individual rock spires are too small to distinguish, but the eroding rhyolitic tuff landscape appears gray. Stream valleys dense with trees and other vegetation, including Rhyolite Canyon and Bonita Canyon, snake across the landscape. With four biogeographic regions converging in the park—the Sonoran Desert, the Chihuahuan Desert, the Rocky Mountains, and the Sierra Madre—it is a haven of plant diversity . Among the 1,000 species growing within the park’s varied desert, grassland, chaparral, deciduous forest, and coniferous forest ecosystems are agaves, prickly pear cacti, yuccas, manzanita, pine, fir, cypress, sycamore, juniper, and oak. The park’s location within the Chiricahua Mountains puts it among several “ sky islands ” in Arizona—isolated mountain ranges that emerge from the surrounding desert “sea.” According to the National Park Service , the range’s highest point (outside the park) rises 2,986 meters (9,795 feet) above sea level, more than 1,800 meters above the surrounding valley. **TITULAR: El cometa PanSTARRS y un meteoro arcoíris iluminan el cielo de noviembre**

**CATEGORÍA: espacio**

El 3 de noviembre de 2026, el fenómeno astronómico del cometa C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) y un meteoro arcoíris han capturado la atención de los astrónomos y entusiastas del cielo. Aunque el meteoro no se originó directamente del cometa, su aparición coincide con el pico de varias lluvias de meteoros, incluyendo las Tauridas del Sur, que alcanzan su cúspide en estos días.

El cometa PanSTARRS, que fue fotografiado en abril desde Hautacam, Francia, destaca por sus impresionantes colas de iones y polvo. Este cometa ha sido objeto de estudio debido a su trayectoria y composición, lo que ha llevado a la comunidad científica a investigar la relación entre cometas y meteoros. Sin embargo, la conexión entre el meteoro arcoíris y el cometa sigue siendo incierta, ya que miles de cometas han pasado por el Sistema Solar interno recientemente.

Durante noviembre, los observadores del cielo también esperan la famosa lluvia de meteoros de los Leonidas, que alcanzará su máximo en aproximadamente dos semanas, ofreciendo más oportunidades para disfrutar de estos espectáculos celestiales.

Comet PanSTARRs and Rainbow Meteor Explanation: Did this meteor come from that comet? Probably not. Although many meteors do originate from comets, there are thousands of comets that have visited the inner Solar System recently, and matching meteors to them can be tricky. And to be clear, the pictured comet is far behind the streaking meteor . Comet C/2025 R3 (PanSTARRS) was captured from Hautacam , France in April when the giant space iceberg sported impressive ion (blue) and dust tails . Sand-sized rocky debris that enters Earth’s atmosphere typically appears as meteors , while the colorful foreground streak here may indicate a complicated composition. This month three notable meteor showers will reach their peaks. Over the next few days, the Southern Taurids will be reaching their apex, while the Northern Taurids will top out about a week later. Both originate from Comet 2P/Encke . November is most famous for the Leonids Meteor Shower , though, which originates from Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle and will reach its crescendo in about two weeks. **TITULAR: Noche en un planeta espeluznante: Auroras y actividad geotérmica en Islandia**

En la noche del 31 de octubre de 2026, un fenómeno natural deslumbrante iluminó el cielo de Hverir, un área geotérmicamente activa en el noreste de Islandia. La combinación de tormentas geomagnéticas, provocadas por la actividad solar, generó auroras boreales que danzaron sobre el paisaje volcánico, creando un espectáculo visual que evocó la atmósfera de Halloween.

Las partículas energéticas, atrapadas en el campo magnético terrestre, penetraron la atmósfera en latitudes altas, produciendo un despliegue de luces verdes y moradas. Este fenómeno se intensificó debido a que el Sol se encuentra en las primeras fases de declive de su ciclo de actividad solar, lo que sugiere que la actividad auroral podría continuar en los próximos días.

Los fumaroles de Hverir, que emiten vapor y gases, se convirtieron en un telón de fondo perfecto para las luces del norte, creando una escena casi fantasmagórica. Este evento no solo atrae a turistas y fotógrafos, sino que también resalta la interconexión entre la actividad solar y los fenómenos geológicos en nuestro planeta.

**TITULAR: Felices 65 años: El Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA antes y ahora**

El 1 de noviembre de 2026, el Centro Espacial Johnson de la NASA celebró su 65 aniversario, un hito que resalta su papel fundamental en la exploración espacial humana. Desde su fundación en 1961, el centro ha sido el corazón del programa de vuelos espaciales tripulados de Estados Unidos, apoyando misiones desde el Proyecto Mercury hasta el programa Artemis.

Ubicado en Houston, Texas, el Johnson Space Center alberga a la tripulación de astronautas de América y el Centro de Control de Misión. A lo largo de los años, ha evolucionado para convertirse en un centro de excelencia en vuelos espaciales, adaptándose a las demandas de nuevas tecnologías y misiones. En la actualidad, el centro gestiona el Programa de Órbita Baja de la Tierra y se prepara para futuras misiones a la Luna y más allá, a través de iniciativas como el Programa Orion.

La historia del centro comenzó tras el famoso discurso del presidente John F. Kennedy el 25 de mayo de 1961, donde se comprometió a llevar a un hombre a la Luna antes de que finalizara la década. Desde entonces, el Johnson Space Center ha sido testigo de logros históricos y continúa siendo un pilar en la exploración espacial.

article.source_body: 6 Min Read Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space. As NASA’s human spaceflight programs evolve, Johnson remains at the forefront of these efforts. Houston is home to NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, comprising International Space Station operations and commercial partnerships and destinations in low Earth orbit. For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠ , while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program ⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth. On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F. Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation. Manned Spacecraft Center to Johnson Space Center The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963. Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs. View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Aerial view of NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Space Center Houston in 2025. NASA/James Blair Project Management Building Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974. The main administration building, called Building 2 until 1974, during President Richard Nixon’s visit in 1974. Employees pose for a group photo in front of Building 1 in 2024. NASA/Robert Markowitz Photo taken in 1964 from the main administration building toward the city of Nassau Bay. The same view from roughly the same vantage point in 2026, showing the mature oak trees and the extensive development outside the center’s gates. Neutral buoyancy spacewalk training The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities. Astronaut candidate Anna L. Fisher trains at the Water Immersion Facility in Houston in 1979. Exploration geologists and Artemis science officers Trevor Graff, left, and Angela Garcia carry out a lunar training development run at NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) in Houston. This testing run marked the first time in the Artemis program that two geologists were suited up simultaneously for lunar geology training in the NBL. Lunar Receiving Laboratory (Building 37) To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned. Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory. Building 37 that housed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in May 1969, two months before the first Moon landing. Aerial view of the Lunar Receiving Park built on the site of Building 37 in 2026. NASA/Robert Markowitz A scientist views an Apollo 11 Moon rock at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in 1969. Spacecraft mockup training facilities (Building 9) Construction of Building 9 began in December 1965 and finished in March 1967. The building initially housed the Technical Services Facility. In April 1969, workers converted a portion of the building to include a mock lunar surface scene, complete with a mockup of a Lunar Module, used by Apollo 11 astronauts. To support the space shuttle program, workers completed an addition that housed the Mockup and Integration Laboratory in September 1974. Astronauts for all 135 shuttle missions used the mockups for training. An extension on the northwest side of thebuilding begun in 1986 and completed in 1988. It received mockups of Space Station Freedom and later of the International Space Station, and the building was renamed the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility. Today, the facility also houses training mockups of NASA’s Orion spacecraft, commercial mockups, and the Active Response Gravity Offload System, known as ARGOS. Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong, left, and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin train for their lunar spacewalk in Building 9 in April 1969. The Space Vehicle Mockup Facility in Building 9 in 2026 NASA/Robert Markowitz Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise trains for his lunar spacewalk in Building 29 using the six-degrees of freedom simulator in January 1970. In the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility in Building 9 in 2026, NASA astronaut Nicole Mann evaluates a new spacesuit design using the Active Response Gravity Offload System, or ARGOS. NASA/David DeHoyos Mission Simulation and Training Facility (Building 5) Construction of Building 5 , the Mission Simulation and Training Facility completed inApril 1965 and began supporting missions beginning with Gemini IV in June 1965. The building originally contained the Gemini spacecraft simulator and a Gemini translation and docking simulator. Apollo program simulators, including a command module and lunar module simulator, began arriving in December 1965. From 1967 and 1978, astronauts used the Water Immersion Facility for spacewalk training. In the early 1970s, the building also housed full-scale, high-fidelity trainers and simulators of Skylab’s components, which all nine Skylab astronauts used for mission training. In the late 1970s, the facility underwent major renovations to support the space shuttle program, with the addition of fixed base and motion base simulators. The Space Station Training Facility addition, completed in 1991, supported first Space Station Freedom and now International Space Station crew training, and also contains Orion and Starliner simulators. The Gemini Translation and Docking Simulator in Building 5 in March 1965 used for astronauts to train on docking with Agena target vehicles. NASA astronauts Stephanie Wilson, left, Jonny Kim, and Randy Bresnik inspect the Orion spacecraft simulator in Building 5 in 2022. NASA/Radislav Sinyak Mission Control Center Construction of Building 30 housing the Mission Control Center began in June 1963 and finished in November 1964, with technicians installing the real-time computer in April 1964 and the first employees moving in two months later. The center initially housed two mission operations control rooms to support Gemini and Apollo missions and simulations. By January 1965, the center monitored the uncrewed Gemini 2 mission and the crewed Gemini 3 mission in a flight following mode. In June 1965, Houston had full control of Gemini IV and has controlled each of NASA’s human space flight missions ever since. The control center received a major upgrade to its computer systems in the mid-1970s to support upcoming space shuttle flights. On April 4, 2011, the building was renamed the Christopher C. Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center, in honor of the man who created the concepts still in use today in human spaceflight control. The control center continues to support the space station around the clock as well as Artemis missions taking humans back to the Moon. The exterior of Building 30 that houses the Mission Control Center during final stages of construction in September 1964. Building 30 in 2026, showing the space station building expansion at left and the plaque naming the facility after Christopher Kraft. NASA/Sumer Loggins Flight Control Room 1 at the Mission Control Center during the Gemini IV mission in June 1965, the first mission control from Houston. NASA’s Artemis II flight control team works on console in the White Flight Control Room in the Mission Control Center during the mission’s lunar flyby on April 6, 2026.
